notes.meaning: David asks God to rescue and protect him from enemies who want to harm him. The Hebrew idea behind protecting him means placing him high up where danger cannot reach. David leans on his personal covenant bond with God when enemies surround his home.

David cries out to be saved from violent men who are eager to kill him. He piles up his requests because his danger is urgent and King Saul's guards are closing in. Believers can bring their most desperate moments straight to God in honest prayer.

Men lie in ambush like wild animals waiting to take David's life. He insists that he did nothing wrong to cause Saul's hatred or provoke an attack. He does not claim to be completely sinless before God, but he is innocent of treason against the king.

The attackers rush quickly into position to strike, even though David gave them no reason to harm him. David calls on God to wake up, come meet him, and see what is happening. God never sleeps, but prayer boldly asks Him to step in and act.

David calls upon God as the Lord of hosts, who commands all heavenly and earthly armies. He asks God to rise up and judge both hostile nations and treacherous people at home who act like pagans. He prays that those who stubbornly plot evil will receive no divine favor for their rebellion.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this prayer as a response to a foreign military invasion, such as the Scythian raids in the time of King Josiah, rather than Saul's soldiers.

notes.meaning: David describes his enemies returning at evening to watch his house and prowl around the city. He compares them to packs of noisy, wild street dogs hunting for prey. Their persistence shows how hungry they are to carry out their evil plans.

Harsh words and slanders pour out of the mouths of David's enemies like water bursting from a spring. Their threats cut like sharp swords because they foolishly assume no one, not even God, hears them. People who forget God is listening quickly lose all restraint in what they say.

The Lord laughs at the arrogant plans of these enemies and treats them with scorn. Saul's men look powerful to human eyes, but against the Almighty their plots are completely helpless. God easily turns the schemes of proud nations into foolishness.

David resolves to look to God rather than tremble before his enemy's strength. He knows that God is his fortress and high place of safety. Looking to the Lord gives quiet confidence even when powerful forces gather outside.

David trusts that the God of faithful love will come out to meet him before danger overwhelms him. God will arrive in time to let him look down on his defeated foes without fear. God's mercy always moves faster than the traps laid by enemies.

David asks God not to kill the attackers right away, so the people of Israel will not quickly forget the lesson. Instead, he asks God to scatter them and make them wander in disgrace as a visible warning. David desires God's justice to instruct his people, not merely to settle a private grudge.

David prays that the wicked will be trapped in the very net of their own arrogant speech. They constantly speak curses, lies, and slander against the innocent. In God's justice, proud words eventually recoil on those who utter them.

David calls for God's judgment to consume the wicked until their power is completely gone. Their downfall will prove to everyone that God truly rules over Israel and across the entire earth. God's judgments ultimately put His supreme glory on display for all nations to see.

David repeats the picture of his enemies returning at evening and snarling like dogs around the city. This time, he speaks with calm confidence, knowing their night patrols cannot succeed against God. What seemed terrifying earlier has now become an empty and failed threat.

The wicked wander around searching for food, growling when they find nothing to eat. They cannot find David to harm him because God has placed him out of their reach. Greed and malice always end up frustrated and unsatisfied.

While his enemies howl in the darkness and leave empty-handed, David wakes up singing in the morning. He praises God's power and faithful love because God proved to be his strong shelter in the hour of trouble. Joy greets the believer when God turns a night of fear into a morning of safety.

David closes his song with direct praise to God, calling Him his strength, his high fortress, and the God of his mercy. He recognizes that any safety or courage he experienced came completely from the Lord. True worship gives all the credit for deliverance to God alone.
